summary: Provides basic terminology for constrained-node networks, in which small devices have severe limits on power, memory, and processing. The terms, such as device classes by capability, have been useful in standardization work on the Internet of Things.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo gives shared terms for small devices and networks with limited resources. It classifies device capabilities and describes ways that energy limits affect communication.

questions: what are class 0 1 and 2 constrained devices
what is the difference between constrained and challenged networks
subtitle: Definitions for constrained nodes and networks, device capability classes, and power use.

tldr.problem: Internet protocols are used on devices and networks with limited power, memory, processing, bandwidth, and connectivity, so standards work needs consistent terminology.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines constrained-node terms, gives rough device classes, and describes energy limits and communication power strategies.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational terminology reference, not a protocol. The memo expects device-class boundaries to move over time.

today: RFC 7228 is an Informational document published in May 2014. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the document provides terminology and notes that device-class boundaries may shift.

sections.title: Why Constrained-Node Terms Are Needed
sections.content:
Small devices with limited processing, memory, or power can connect to the Internet and form networks. Those networks may also have unreliable links, limited bandwidth, or changing connections. The memo provides a set of core terms so groups working on these environments can use words consistently.

In this document, “byte” means octet, “KiB” means 1024 bytes, and “power” means electrical power unless stated otherwise. “Mains-powered” means continuously connected to a stable electrical power grid.
sections.plainLanguage: Small connected devices and their networks have limits that ordinary computers may not have. Shared terms help people describe those limits consistently.

sections.title: Constrained Nodes and Networks
sections.content:
A constrained node cannot meet some characteristics normally expected of Internet nodes, often because of cost or physical limits. Limits on power, memory, and processing can restrict code, stored state, and computation. A constrained network lacks some link-layer characteristics commonly expected on the Internet; examples include low throughput, variable packet loss, asymmetric links, penalties for large packets, and limited multicast.

A constrained-node network is influenced by having a significant portion of constrained nodes and is therefore also a constrained network. A challenged network has serious difficulty maintaining the end-to-end IP model, for example because of long interruptions or delays beyond TCP's Maximum Segment Lifetime. All challenged networks are constrained, but not all constrained networks are challenged. The memo also discusses LLN and LoWPAN/6LoWPAN as related terms without defining them.
sections.plainLanguage: A constrained node has limited resources; a constrained network has limited communication features. A challenged network has more serious difficulty maintaining end-to-end Internet communication.

sections.title: Classes of Constrained Devices
sections.content:
The memo gives rough classes based on data size, such as RAM, and code size, such as Flash. Class 0 devices are very limited and will generally need larger devices to act as proxies, gateways, or servers. Class 1 devices may not easily run full protocol stacks such as HTTP and TLS, but can use stacks designed for constrained nodes and can participate without a gateway. Class 2 devices can support most stacks used on notebooks or servers, though lightweight protocols may still help.

The class values reflect device clusters at the time of writing, and the memo expects their boundaries to move. It defines no classes beyond Class 2 because devices with greater capabilities can largely use existing protocols unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: Class 0 devices usually need another device to communicate on their behalf. Class 1 devices can use a smaller protocol stack, while Class 2 devices can support most familiar stacks.

sections.title: Energy Limits and Communication Strategies
sections.content:
The memo recommends describing available power as sustainable average power Ps, measured in watts, and available total energy Et, measured in joules. It defines energy classes by when energy runs out: E0 for a specific event, E1 for a period, E2 over the device lifetime, and E9 when no direct quantitative energy limit applies.

It describes three communication strategies. P0 (normally-off) devices sleep for long periods and reattach when they wake. P1 (low-power) devices use very little power but retain some network attachment, potentially with high latency. P9 (always-on) devices remain connected. Duty cycling means periodically switching a function off and on to save power.
sections.plainLanguage: Energy labels describe whether a device has power for one event, one period, its lifetime, or no direct limit. Communication labels describe whether it disconnects, stays attached while saving power, or remains on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo introduces terminology and says it raises no new security issues. Security effects of resource constraints must be considered in the context of specific protocols. It points to discussion of constrained-node security in CoAP, threat analysis for RPL, and work on implementing security protocols on constrained nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: The vocabulary itself does not add security risks. Each protocol still needs to address the security effects of the devices' and networks' limits.
